title: The Gaseous State — Characteristics and Measurable Properties
notes: What defines a gas and the four measurable variables (P, V, T, n) whose relationships the gas laws and kinetic theory explain — the orientation before the postulates.
### Defining characteristics of the gaseous state
• No fixed shape or volume — a gas fills its container completely.
• Very low density compared with liquids/solids (air ≈ 1.3 kg m⁻³ vs water 1000 kg m⁻³); highly compressible; diffuse rapidly.
• Molecules are far apart (intermolecular distances ≈ 10 molecular diameters at STP) with negligible attraction — hence expansion and compressibility.
• Exerts pressure uniformly in all directions (momentum transfer on wall collisions).
• Mixes completely and homogeneously (diffusion, effusion through pinholes).
• **Pressure (P):** force per unit area; units Pa (N m⁻²), atm (1 atm = 101325 Pa = 760 mm Hg), bar (1 bar = 10⁵ Pa); measured with barometers/manometers.
• **Temperature (T):** kelvin only in gas laws; T(K) = t(°C) + 273.15.
• **Amount (n):** moles; links to mass via molar mass and to particles via N_A.

Boyle (P–V at fixed T), Charles (V–T at fixed P), Gay-Lussac (P–T at fixed V), Avogadro (V–n at fixed P, T), combined equation and PV = nRT. Each law fixes two variables and studies the other two — the 'constant-holding' logic of all gas-law experiments.
### Why gases need a molecular model

The measured regularities (PV = nRT for all gases at low P) are too universal to be accidental: they point to a common microscopic structure. The kinetic theory supplies it — postulates → PV = ⅓mnc̄² → PV = nRT — and its idealisations (point molecules, no attraction) mark exactly where real gases deviate.
confusion: ❌ Gases have negligible mass. ✅ They have small but definite mass — 22.4 L of air weighs about 29 g at STP.
❌ Temperature in gas laws may be taken in °C. ✅ Absolute (kelvin) temperature only; 0 °C is 273.15 K.
❌ A gas exerts pressure only downward. ✅ Pressure is isotropic — equal in every direction.

universalFacts: Air is a mixture (78% N₂, 21% O₂, ~1% Ar/CO₂) that behaves nearly ideally at 1 atm — the everyday ideal gas.
One mole of any gas at STP occupies 22.4 L and, for air, weighs ≈28.97 g (average molar mass).
The mean free path at 1 atm is ≈10⁻⁷ m — molecules travel ~1000 diameters between collisions.
examples: **Problem:** Express 2.5 atm in mm Hg and Pa. **Solution:** 2.5 × 760 = 1900 mm Hg; 2.5 × 101325 = 253 312 Pa ≈ 2.53 × 10⁵ Pa.

summary: A gas has no fixed shape or volume and fills its container completely; it has a very low density, being highly compressible and diffusing rapidly, its molecules are far apart with negligible attraction, it exerts pressure uniformly in all directions, and it mixes completely and homogeneously by diffusion and effusion. The four measurable state variables are pressure in Pa, atm or bar, volume, absolute temperature in kelvin, and amount in moles, and the gas laws are the pairwise relations among them at fixed T, P, V or n. Because PV = nRT holds so universally for gases at low pressure, the behaviour points to a common microscopic structure, which the kinetic theory supplies and whose idealisations mark exactly where real gases deviate.

keyPoints: Fix the four variables P, V, T and n in mind before the laws — every law is a two-at-a-time relation among them.
Use kelvin always; the °C slip is the classic numerical error.
Low density and high compressibility both follow from molecules being far apart with negligible attraction.
Gases mix completely by diffusion and effusion, which is how their compositions are analysed.
The kinetic theory converts these macroscopic regularities into a microscopic model.
specialNotes: Gases do have mass: 22.4 L of air at STP weighs about 29 g, since the average molar mass of air is about 28.97 g mol⁻¹.
The pressure a gas exerts is isotropic, so it is equal in every direction — a common misconception is that it acts only downwards.
The intermolecular distance in a gas at STP is about ten molecular diameters, which is why the gas is mostly empty space.
Because PV = nRT holds for so many different gases at low pressure, the behaviour cannot be accidental and must reflect a common structure.
Molar volumes of liquid water and of a gas at STP differ enormously, so gas laws must never be applied to liquids or solids.
